title_original: The Intricate Photographic Techniques of Sally Mann

blocks.text: Born in 1951 in Lexington, Virginia, where she still lives and works, Sally Mann has made the American South, with its landscapes, its ghosts and its history of violence, the subject of a body of work spanning more than four decades. She first drew wide attention with At Twelve (1988), portraits of adolescent girls, then with Immediate Family (1992), intimate and sometimes unsettling images of her three children growing up on the family farm, which brought her both fame and fierce controversy. Working with an 8×10 view camera, she later turned to the 19th-century wet-plate collodion process, whose flaws, streaks and accidents became part of her vocabulary in series such as “Deep South” and “What Remains,” a meditation on death and decay. In 2015, she published Hold Still , a memoir that was a finalist for the National Book Award. Her retrospective “A Thousand Crossings” opened at the National Gallery of Art in Washington in 2018 before traveling to the Jeu de Paume in Paris in 2019.

This segment comes from “Place,” an episode of the first season of Art21’s documentary series “Art in the Twenty-First Century,” which premiered on PBS in September 2001. Filmed both in her studio and outdoors, it follows Mann at work on the farm where she lives, which serves as both the backdrop and the subject of her photographs.
